PDDL-Mind: Large Language Models are Capable
on Belief Reasoning with Reliable State Tracking

Qiutong Tony Yi    Wang Bill ZhuRobin JiaJesse ThomasonUniversity of Southern California Email: {qiutongy, wangzhu, robinjia, jessetho}@usc.edu
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) perform substantially below human level on existing theory-of-mind (ToM) benchmarks, even when augmented with chain-of-thought prompting or probabilistic belief updates. We argue that these failures primarily arise from unreliable implicit state tracking rather than limitations in high-level reasoning. We introduce PDDL-Mind, a neuro-symbolic framework that decouples environment state evolution from belief inference. By translating narrative descriptions into explicit states and actions expressed in Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), and by verifying action-induced state transitions against a predefined domain, PDDL-Mind provides LLMs with a logically consistent and explicit representation of world states for ToM tasks. Experiments on MMToM-QA and MuMa-ToM and FanToM show that PDDL-Mind achieves over 5%5\% absolute accuracy gain over the best existing state-of-the-art method on ToM benchmark questions.

†† ∗  Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Theory-of-Mind (ToM) benchmarks present narratives in which agents act in the world and observers must infer what those agents believe, know, or intend. These narratives typically take one of two forms: descriptions of physical actions in an environment, or dialogue transcripts between agents. These variations share a common underlying structure: each narrative is fundamentally a sequence of events that induces a sequence of world states Huang et al. (2024a); Xu et al. (2025).

Frontier large language models (LLMs) continue to perform substantially below human level on these ToM tasks Jin et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2025). There is no consensus on the root cause of these failures. Broadly, two competing hypotheses have emerged. The first attributes errors to state tracking: models fail to maintain accurate representations of world states as events accumulate over time. The second attributes errors to reasoning: models track the progression of events adequately, but fail during the subsequent inference of beliefs or intentions from those states Huang et al. (2024a). Works from both isles admit ToM benchmark instances can be partitioned into chains of events, yet leave the notion of an event unanalyzed beyond surface segmentation. We argue that a deeper understanding the nature of events permits proper disentanglement of these hypotheses.

We draw insight from neo-Davidsonian event semantics. In the neo-Davidsonian view: “Mary lifted the cup to the kitchen,” “Mary walked with the cup,” and “Mary moved something” may all be true of a single occurrence Schein (2012); Kratzer (2023). Defining a verb means specifying the event’s preconditions and effects. Events thus provide a level of abstraction above linguistic variation, a stable referent that diverse verb phrases can converge on.

Motivated by this observation, a programming language that places emphasis on predicate definition is a natural substrate to augment LLMs’ event perception and tracking. We introduce PDDL-Mind, a framework that provides a reliable and explicit state-tracking mechanism for ToM narratives. Starting from a predefined Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL, Ghallab et al., 1998) domain file with 7 general action types, we use an LLM to parse the initial environment description into a PDDL problem file and to translate narrative events into a sequence of PDDL actions. We then verify each action by checking its preconditions and executing valid transitions within the domain, filtering out invalid actions. As a result, we obtain a logically consistent sequence of world states, which we manually verified to be correct in 90%90\% of cases. Finally, we provide this verified state sequence to the LLM and evaluate it solely on ToM inference questions.

PDDL-Mind with GPT-4o achieves 88.3%88.3\% accuracy on MMToM-QA and 88.8%88.8\% accuracy on MuMa-ToM, using only 3 LLM calls per example. Both outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method, AutoToM Zhang et al. (2025), which requires an average of 27 LLM calls per example, by more than 5%5\%. These results provide strong evidence that unreliable state tracking, rather than insufficient reasoning capacity, is the primary bottleneck in current ToM evaluations of LLMs.

2 PDDL-Mind

We introduce PDDL-Mind, a neuro-symbolic framework that decouples environment state evolution from belief inference (Figure 1).

Predefined domain file.

We begin with a predefined PDDL domain file. The design is motivated by the structure of existing textual ToM benchmarks, which pose ToM questions after presenting narratives in one of two forms: descriptions of physical actions in an environment, or dialogue transcripts between agents.

We define four object types in the domain: agent, representing people mentioned in the narrative (e.g., “Mary”); loc, representing locations in the environment (e.g., “bathroom”); obj, representing physical items (e.g., “apple”); and utterance, representing spoken messages in the narrative (e.g., “Mary has a golden retriever”). We then define a set of predicates to describe domain states, such as at, in, and holding. Crucially, we introduce the predicate seen to track whether an object is observed by an agent, and heard to track whether an utterance is heard by an agent. Finally, we define seven actions: move, open, close, grab, drop, ask, and tell, each with explicitly specified parameters, preconditions, and postconditions. The complete PDDL domain file is provided in Appendix C.

State and action extraction.

Given the domain file, we first prompt an LLM to parse the narrative into a PDDL problem file, which specifies the objects present in the environment and the initial state s0s_{0}. We define a state ss as a set of grounded predicates, such as (at Mary bathroom). We find this step to be relatively straightforward for frontier LLMs, because most ToM benchmarks describe simple, small-scale environments.

Next, using both the domain file and the generated problem file, the LLM parses the narrative into a sequence of candidate actions (a1,…,at)(a_{1},\dots,a_{t}). Because narratives may include events that cannot be mapped to PDDL actions (e.g., “steps near the sink”), we filter the generated action sequence post-hoc to retain only valid actions. For each candidate action aia_{i}, if the current state si−1s_{i-1} satisfies the action’s preconditions, we accept the action and apply its postconditions to produce the next state sis_{i}. Otherwise, the action is ignored and not executed. This process yields a verified sequence of actions and corresponding world states.

ToM question answering.

The LLM is provided with the verified state sequence and a ToM question, and is asked to perform inference in a chain-of-thought manner. By conditioning inference on explicitly verified states, PDDL-Mind isolates ToM reasoning from errors in implicit state tracking.

We provide additional details on the design of domain files in the next subsection.

3 Experiment results

We evaluate PDDL-Mind on three representative ToM benchmarks, spanning single and multi agent settings: MMToM-QA Jin et al. (2024), which contains 600 examples focusing on long-context action sequence belief and goal inference, MuMa-ToM Shi et al. (2024), which contains 900 examples targeting belief and goal inference in multi-agent action/conversation sequences, and FanToM Kim et al. (2023), which contains 10K questions alongside 256 instances in multi-agent conversational belief inference. Each ToM task is a multi-choice question answering evaluated by accuracy. We compare against five representative baselines: BIP-ALM Jin et al. (2024) and LIMP Shi et al. (2024), which combine Bayesian Inverse Planning with LLMs, with BIP-ALM performing explicit belief updates while LIMP does not; TT Kim et al. (2025), which traces agents’ mental states by generating and weighting hypotheses based on observations; AutoToM Zhang et al. (2025), which iteratively constructs and refines agent models tailored to each ToM task; and EnigmaToM Xu et al. (2025), which tracks events using a neural knowledge base.

PDDL-Mind provides reliable state tracking.

We report average accuracy for all methods evaluated with GPT-4o OpenAI (2024) in Table 1. PDDL-Mind outperforms all baselines on both benchmarks, achieving accuracy improvements of more than 5.3%5.3\% on MMToM-QA and 7.4%7.4\% on MuMa-ToM. To directly assess state-tracking quality, we manually inspect 20 verified action sequences per benchmark and find that 36 out of 40 (90%90\%) are correct and fully consistent with the narratives. While all baselines incorporate some form of state tracking, these results indicate that their implicit or heuristic mechanisms are substantially less reliable than the explicit verification used in PDDL-Mind.

PDDL-Mind is cost-efficient.

PDDL-Mind requires only three LLM calls per example, whereas all baseline methods in Table 1 require an order of magnitude more calls. For instance, AutoToM reports an average of 17.6 LLM calls per example on MMToM-QA and 35.1 calls on MuMa-ToM. These results demonstrate that reliable state tracking can be achieved without increased inference cost, and in fact leads to significantly more efficient evaluation.

Remaining errors reflect both parsing and reasoning limitations.

Despite its strong performance, PDDL-Mind still exhibits an error rate of approximately 12%12\% when evaluated with GPT-4o. We manually analyze 20 failure cases per benchmark and find that 13 cases (33%33\%) stem from parsing errors that produce incorrect action sequences, while the remaining 67%67\% are due to genuine reasoning failures given correct states. This analysis suggests that, under perfect state tracking, the error rate would drop to approximately 8%8\%, further supporting the claim that state tracking is the dominant bottleneck in current ToM evaluations. We provide qualitative examples in Appendix D.2.

PDDL-Mind yields consistent gains across models and categories.

We further compare PDDL-Mind against more cost-efficient ToM approaches, including vanilla chain-of-thought (CoT), which uses a single LLM call per instance, and DWM Huang et al. (2024a), which partitions narratives into chunks and queries mental states after each segment. As shown in Table 2, PDDL-Mind consistently outperforms these baselines across nearly all sub-categories of MMToM-QA and MuMa-ToM and across different model backbones. The sole exception is the Belief category on MuMa-ToM when using Claude-Sonnet-4.5 Anthropic (2024), where both PDDL-Mind and DWM exceed 95%95\% accuracy, with DWM outperforming by a modest margin of 3.3%3.3\%. Further manual inspection reveals that, at such high accuracy levels, residual parsing errors disproportionately limit gains.

4 Structural Abstraction of ToM Benchmarks

Figure 2 summarizes the underlying structure of ToM benchmark instances through three complementary views, with colors denoting timesteps.

Single-agent action sequences (left panel).

The left panel illustrates a typical single-agent Sally–Anne scenario. Consider the narrative:

Alice is in the kitchen and opens the fridge, moves to the cabinet and opens it, she moves to the living room, and opens the cabinet there.

The colored events correspond to transitions in the left panel of Figure 2. Such instances admit a hierarchical (tree-structured) interpretation: the environment induces a containment structure in which houses contain rooms, rooms contain containers, and containers may contain objects. Each action updates either the agent’s location within this hierarchy or their perceptual access (e.g., opening a container).

State tracking reduces to maintaining the agent’s position in this structure and recording visibility at each node. Computationally, this corresponds to structured traversal with local state updates, which is reflected in our domain design.

Multi-agent conversation (right panel).

The right panel extends this structural view to multi-agent settings. We model conversation as broadcast within a shared environment: when an agent speaks, all currently present agents receive and store the utterance. State transitions are therefore defined by how memories evolve over time, independent of the truth value of the utterances. Agents may leave (ceasing to receive updates) or join mid-conversation (receiving only subsequent information).

Concretely:

Alice: “I hope everyone is doing well!”
Billy: “I need to leave now, talk to you later!”
Cliff: “Hope I’m not interrupting!”
David: “Of course you’re not!”

Reading the right panel top-to-bottom, each row is a timestep and each column an agent present at that time. Speech acts induce broadcast edges from the speaker to all listeners, while join/leave events modify the set of recipients.

This interaction structure is not strictly hierarchical; instead, it is better understood as evolving information flow over a dynamically changing set of agents. It can be naturally encoded using predicate-based updates such as Speak, Hear, Present, Join, and Leave.

A unified event–state abstraction (middle panel).

The middle panel captures a minimal abstraction shared across ToM benchmarks: a sequence of states (nodes) connected by events (edges), read from top to bottom. This view factors out linguistic variation and isolates the core dynamics that models must track.

Within a unified PDDL formulation, both physical actions and conversational updates are treated as events with preconditions and effects, yielding a consistent and inherently multi-agent representation.

Overall, the left panel corresponds to hierarchical state tracking (as in MMToM), the right panel captures multi-agent information flow (as in FanToM), and the middle panel highlights the shared event-driven abstraction that PDDL-Mind generalizes across both settings.

5 Related Work

Riemer et al. (2025) distinguishes literal ToM (accurately verbalizing another agent’s beliefs given context) from functional ToM (adapting one’s policy based on such inferences). We address literal ToM.

Dynamics of implicit wagers in inference-time augmentation.

Inference-time augmentation methods that do not modify model weights share a common incentive: eliciting structure the model is assumed to already possess. This division of labor places an implicit wager that the language model has capability CC: if it does, performance improves; if not, no scaffold compensates, since there is no more-intelligent system to fall back on. Our results suggest a more favorable wager: separating state tracking from reasoning. Language models reliably parse into constrained symbolic forms and perform variable binding Wu et al. (2025); Prakash et al. (2025), particularly for PDDL Liu et al. (2023); Zhu et al. (2025); we situate our approach in this regime.

Probabilistic methods.

One family wagers on numerical confidence estimates. AutoToM Zhang et al. (2025) and BIP-ALM Jin et al. (2024) require LM logits over actions conditioned on hypothesized goals and beliefs, then aggregate via Bayes’ rule across timesteps. ThoughtTracing Kim et al. (2025) assigns each hypothesis a numerical weight by mapping LLM categorical likelihood judgments to fixed scores, tuning favorability under random resampling. These approaches hinge on LLMs inducing a coherent probability measure over action–goal–belief triples, calibrated to track the diagnosticity of evidence; such measures remain implicit in the training distribution Huang et al. (2024b). We hypothesize a second architectural hazard: when scalar comparison is the sole intermediate arbiter, upstream linguistic richness cannot overcome a numerical bottleneck at the decision point—information that does not separate the scalar cannot affect the outcome, regardless of how richly it was represented moments before. PDDL-Mind avoids this bottleneck by preserving linguistic structure throughout inference, aligning with discrete methods.

Discrete state methods.

Partially sidestepping these hazards, DWM Huang et al. (2024a), EnigmaToM Xu et al. (2025), and PDDL-Mind embrace discreteness by parsing natural language into symbolic representations while assuming deterministic transition rules. DWM and EnigmaToM place two wagers: that neural models can identify state-relevant events and correctly infer the transition rules. Our work shows the second wager is unnecessary. The transition semantics of ToM benchmarks are fully specified by their verb inventories, with explicit preconditions and effects; asking a model to “discover” what a benchmark already defines invites hallucination and inconsistency.

Textual ToM benchmarks.

A large body of theory-of-mind benchmarks are purely textual, including ToMi Le et al. (2019), BigToM Gandhi et al. (2023), Hi-ToM Wu et al. (2023), FanToM Kim et al. (2023), OpenToM Xu et al. (2024), and NegotiationToM Chan et al. (2024). We did not test on all of these benchmarks, as they all share a common narrative structure: each presents a sequence of events in one of two forms—descriptions of physical actions within an environment, or dialogue transcripts between agents. Moreover, results from prior methods (e.g., AutoToM) indicate that several benchmarks, such as ToMi and BigToM, are already saturated, limiting their utility for distinguishing model capabilities.

Prompting-based ToM methods.

Prior prompting-based approaches to ToM emphasize the apparent limitations of LLMs in mental-state reasoning. For instance, SymbolicToM Sclar et al. (2023) constructs explicit belief graphs for each character, SimToM Wilf et al. (2024) filters narratives to retain only events observable to a target agent before prompting, and TimeToM Hou et al. (2024) augments stories with explicit temporal structure. Although superficially similar, PDDL-Mind is grounded in a fundamentally different perspective: LLMs are capable of theory-of-mind reasoning, but are primarily limited by unreliable state tracking. This perspective finds theoretical grounding in GEPA’s Agrawal et al. (2025) principle of competence-aligned scaffolding. Effective augmentation identifies what the model performs reliably and externalizes the rest. LLMs interpret linguistic feedback productively but learn poorly from scalar gradients; GEPA accordingly shifts learning to language-based reflection. LLMs reason over explicit states adequately but recover states from narrative variation unreliably; PDDL-Mind accordingly shifts state tracking to verified PDDL transitions. Enabling substantially improved ToM inference.

6 Conclusion

We show that current LLM failures on ToM tasks primarily reflect unreliable implicit state tracking rather than deficiencies in high-level reasoning, and that PDDL untangling isolates this bottleneck. We therefore argue that future ToM benchmarks should treat accurate, verifiable state tracking as a prerequisite for meaningful assessment. Broader philosophical implications of this disentanglement are discussed in Appendix A.

Implications for benchmark structure.

Across existing ToM benchmarks, tree-like structure frequently emerges as a convenient abstraction for tracking event effects. This prevalence reflects implicit inductive biases: (i) Sally–Anne-style action narratives assume a hierarchical, containment-based world, and (ii) conversational benchmarks impose a fixed temporal order that yields an acyclic update structure.

Recognizing these biases, and the fact that trees are a strict subset of graphs, allows us to impose a stronger structural constraint on ToM state-tracking models than prior graph-based formulations such as Xu et al. (2025), which treat entity dynamics more generally. At the same time, this perspective highlights a limitation of current benchmarks: their structural regularities may enable success via symbolic state tracking alone. We therefore advocate for future benchmark designs that move beyond these biases to better probe robust and generalizable ToM reasoning.

Limitations

PDDL-Mind operates entirely on textual inputs and symbolic abstractions, and therefore does not address multimodal ToM scenarios involving visual, spatial, or embodied perception. Extending the framework to grounded or multimodal environments would require integrating perception modules and aligning their outputs with symbolic state representations, which is beyond the scope of this work.

Our approach also relies on a predefined PDDL domain, which introduces brittleness for weaker models that struggle to correctly parse narratives into symbolic actions and states. While frontier models handle this parsing reliably in our experiments, improving robustness for smaller or less capable models remains an open challenge.

Appendix

Appendix A Philosophical Implications

This section discusses philosophical implications of disentangling state tracking from belief inference.

Complexity frameworks such as Huang et al. (2024a) propose that the complexity of theory-of-mind tasks can be characterized by the number of states an observer must track. This view presupposes that a task comes with a natural partition into discrete states. We argue that such partitions exist only under specific structural conditions, and that making these conditions explicit clarifies both the scope and the limits of rigorous ToM evaluation.

Inferring artistic intention from a painting is itself a theory-of-mind task. Consider Picasso’s Lover in a Beret in Figure 3. If asked to interpret Picasso’s intentions, a typical human viewer may first recognize a human face in the center of the frame. This recognition constitutes immediate progress toward attributing an intention (to depict a face), after which the viewer can further decompose the face into subcomponents (e.g., nose, eyes) and stylistic distortions characteristic of cubist portraiture.

However, human face’s physiology is shaped by millennia of selection pressures under Earth’s conditions. Now imagine presenting the same painting to an alien with human-comparable intelligence but whose evolution under a distinct environment yields no facial similarity to humans. If the alien has never encountered a human face, it is unreasonable to expect even the shallow interpretations that humans with the requisite background knowledge achieve effortlessly. Instead, the alien may rely on a more basic representation: geometric properties of the image, trajectories of lines and curves, enclosed shapes, and relations among regions. The alien is likely to form a partition of the painting starkly different from Figure 3. One might argue that humans also use geometric information—perhaps passing through a geometric stage before recognizing that a face is a face and a nose is a nose. If so, the earlier depiction of interpretation omitted several intermediate steps: humans compress many geometric primitives into a single semantic unit. The curves and angles undergo a gestalt transformation and was assigned contingent hierarchies by a viewer who possesses the concept “face.”

This thought experiment poses a challenge for state-counting approaches to ToM complexity. The same painting induces markedly different state representations depending on the observer’s conceptual vocabulary. For a human, the painting may involve tracking a small number of semantic units (face, expression, background). For the alien, it may require tracking many more geometric primitives. If the number of states depends on the observer in this way, state counts cannot be treated as an intrinsic property of the task. Instead, the partitioning procedure that produces those states—and its upstream epistemological commitments—becomes the central object of analysis. Complexity derived from state statistics is thus observer-relative, and cross-observer comparisons lose a clear meaning. Consequently, any benchmark intended to be solvable by state-tracking algorithms alone must eliminate this relativity by fixing the vocabulary relative to which states are individuated.

Fixing a vocabulary and its update rules effectively encodes an algorithm. Each benchmark specifies, through its verb inventory and the semantics of those verbs, a procedure for computing state transitions. Under such designs, success reduces to recovering this algorithm from narrative input and executing it correctly. ToM evaluation in these settings becomes a form of algorithm recovery. The extent to which world knowledge participates in this recovery process admits a hierarchy. At the minimal end, the algorithm is recoverable from syntax alone. For example, “Mary moves the ball to the basket” encodes agent, object, and destination in its argument structure; a syntactic parse can populate the slots of an update function without requiring knowledge of what moving, balls, or baskets are. Sally–Anne benchmarks often operate near this regime: verb inventories are constrained, syntactic frames are uniform, and the algorithm reduces to maintaining a record of which agents were present when which verbs applied to which arguments. One step beyond syntax, the algorithm requires lexical semantics. Many subjective predicates implicitly parameterize a continuous internal degree whose value is mediated by external context. Modeling such verbs may therefore require representing latent scalar state variables and updating them when relevant external events occur. Because external events can continuously modulate these latent degrees, reliable inference requires explicit tracking of their event-conditioned updates rather than recovering them from narrative surface form alone. More broadly, lexical semantics can introduce additional latent mental variables. For instance, to properly compute hide-related conditions, one may need to track an implicit variable capturing an agent’s aversion to being discovered, maybe even by a specific person. Such transition semantics are not recoverable from syntax alone and often require simulating a world model that includes variables not explicitly present in the predicate parameters. Selecting such variables depends on inductive biases that are not resolved by the more rudimentary structural biases discussed above (tree structure, fixed arrow of time, syntax). Further along the hierarchy, the algorithm requires compositional integration of long-tail world knowledge embedded in narrative form. As with interpreting another agent’s interpretation of Picasso, the same syntactic frame—with identical grammatical roles—can demand different transition semantics depending on what the model knows about domains not explicitly mentioned in the narrative. A character’s reaction may depend on biological inheritance, professional norms, or cultural and historical conventions that no verb encodes. Computing the correct state transition then requires recognizing the relevance of such facts and retrieving them from outside the text.

This hierarchy suggests two directions for benchmark evolution.

First, benchmarks can vary the algorithm associated with a verb across instances. In Sally–Anne-style action sequences, verbs such as “move” typically correspond to a single, uniform update rule (e.g., updating spatial containment). Moreover, many benchmarks admit substantial lexical variation without introducing new transition dynamics: for example, although “leave” differs from “move” in surface form, both effectively denote a change in an agent’s occupied location and therefore reduce to the same underlying state update. Figure 4 illustrates this collapse in MMToM, where 17 of 24 verbs (≈70%\approx 70\%) are functionally equivalent to one of three predefined PDDL actions, while the rest can be safely ignored without compromising the causal fidelity of the parsed action chain. This kind of synonymy lowers the burden of algorithm recovery once a small set of transition rules is learned. A more resistant design would break this uniformity by allowing the same surface verb to realize different transition functions across contexts: “move” in one scenario could update spatial containment, while “move” in another (e.g., chess) updates strategic position. Under identical syntax, the correct algorithm would then be context-dependent, and a system that has learned one interpretation of “move” would not transfer without first identifying which interpretation the current scenario requires. Second, benchmarks can expand the world model so that only systems with human-level integration of long-tail knowledge can answer the questions posed. Certain benchmarks are solvable by symbolic methods because the relevant domain can be fully specified in advance: a PDDL file enumerates predicates, verbs, and update rules. A benchmark that intentionally exceeds this closure would be less amenable to symbolic assistance. BigToM Gandhi et al. (2023) is one example, where language models generate novel instances using long-tail knowledge. However, BigToM is now saturated, with Gemini 2.0 scoring 86.33% and GPT-4o scoring 82.42% Kim et al. (2025). In benchmarks of this kind, correct transitions may depend on facts about genetics, economics, or social convention that cannot be exhaustively enumerated in a domain file. Only a system that has acquired broad world knowledge—a language model or a human—can reliably recognize the relevance of such facts and retrieve them appropriately.

Appendix B Ablations

Two pieces in our design were critical to the pipeline’s success: The predefined domain file and the symbolic verification of states derived from the parsed action sequence. We ablate the two sections respectively on all three benchmarks for GPT-4o. The results are reported in Table 3. For the predefined domain ablation, the model looks at one example per benchmark and generates its own PDDL domain. For the verification ablation, no intermediate states were provided to the language model. We noticed a less-than-expected drop in accuracy in ablation 1. We hypothesize that instances within a benchmark share a considerable amount of structure, and thus even domain file constructed on one few-shot example generalizes to the entire benchmark.

Appendix D Experiment Details

D.1 Implementation Details

For all models and all benchmarks, we use a temperature of 0 and a max token of 4,096 for LLM inference. To avoid data leakage, we stratified the sample 50 examples per sub-category on each benchmark, such that we exclude the examples used to design PDDL domain file and prompt templates.

D.2 Error Analysis

Appendix E Ethics and Risks

Potential risks.

Our method conditions LLMs on a predefined PDDL domain file that specifies permissible actions and state transitions. While this design improves state-tracking reliability, it also introduces potential risks. Broadly, providing structured domain knowledge to LLMs raises the risk that reported performance improvements reflect alignment with the predefined schema rather than intrinsic gains in reasoning ability. To mitigate this, we release the full domain specification and prompts, and encourage future work to evaluate robustness under alternative or extended domain definitions.

Data and model use.

We use public dataset MMToM-QA and MuMa-ToM, which are both under MIT license. Both datasets are anonymized and contain no human private data. GPT-4o (OpenAI) and Claude-4.5-Sonnet (Anthropic) are accessible exclusively via commercial APIs. These systems are governed by restrictive Terms of Service that prohibit model weight extraction, reverse engineering, and competitive distillation, serving to protect their respective architectural innovations and agentic harnesses. Kimi-K2-Instruct operates under a Modified MIT License; this variant permits general commercial use but mandates strictly visible attribution for entities exceeding 100 million monthly active users or $20 million in monthly revenue.

LLM use.

We use LLMs to generate PDDL problem files and action sequences, to answer theory-of-mind questions in our experiments, and to improve writing fluency and correct grammatical errors.
